ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Geriatric Medicine Referral — Mary Seacole — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Visit for headaches on waking and knee pain with a fall: very high blood pressure found, without target-organ emergency; examination, ECG, laboratory tests, home monitoring, knee osteoarthritis, falls screen, her own remedies, and geriatric medicine referral

text.paragraph: A 71-year-old woman living alone with blood pressure 184/102 mmHg and morning headaches, without a hypertensive emergency, bilateral knee osteoarthritis, a fall last year and fear of falling. Please see her at her one-week review for a comprehensive geriatric assessment and advice on blood pressure treatment, falls, her knees and her social needs. [S]
Urgency: Soon; at her one-week review. [S]

list.item: Which blood pressure medicines and target do you advise for her, given her age, living alone and fall risk?
What does the falls assessment show, and what should be done about it?
How should we manage her knee osteoarthritis without oral anti-inflammatory medicines?
Are any of her own remedies a problem with the medicines we plan?
What support do you advise for loneliness, mood, the stairs and the cost of care?

text.paragraph: Mary Seacole, a nurse and healer of long experience who asked to be called Mrs. Seacole, lives alone in rooms up two flights of stairs in Paddington and is careful with money. Morning headaches for three weeks; today 184/102 mmHg (two seated readings, large cuff), pulse 78; no chest pain, breathlessness, visual loss, confusion or weakness; fundi with arteriolar narrowing only; ECG with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage. Laboratory results today: sodium 140, potassium 4.1, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL (eGFR 67), glucose 96, hemoglobin A1c 5.6%, LDL 146 mg/dL, TSH 2.1, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 18 mg/g, hemoglobin 12.8. Home readings with a validated monitor for one week before treatment. Knee pain 6 out of 10 with crepitus and bony enlargement; KOOS JR 52.5; diclofenac gel started. One trip on the outside steps last year, without injury; she now goes out less. BMI 31.6. She uses her own remedies (ginger tea, a liquorice root infusion, a camphor and wintergreen liniment) and chose to pause the liquorice. No other medicines [S]

list.item: She wants to keep walking to see her friends without fear of falling. [S]
She wants her own knowledge as a healer, and her remedies, respected rather than dismissed. [S]
She worries about the cost of medicines and getting to appointments. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: She was born Mary Jane Grant in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1805, the daughter of James Grant, a white Scottish army officer, and a free Black Jamaican woman who kept a boarding house; she was born free, at a time when many Black people in the Caribbean were enslaved, and had a sister, Louisa, and a brother, Edward. In her memoir she wrote that "the century and myself were both young together" and called herself a Creole "with good Scotch blood." [D]
A London commemorative database gives her date of birth as November 23, 1805; English Heritage, the Mary Seacole Trust and her memoir give no day. [D]

Her mother was a healer, "like very many of the Creole women, an admirable doctress," and taught her traditional Jamaican medicine; as a child she practised on her doll, and she later learned "a great deal of Creole medicinal art" in her mother's house. She visited England in the early 1820s and gained some knowledge of European medicine. [D]

She married Edwin Horatio Hamilton Seacole on November 10, 1836, and they kept a store at Black River; he was delicate, she nursed him, and he died in 1844, followed closely by the death of her mother. She had no children. [D]

In 1850 she nursed victims of the cholera epidemic in Kingston, learning about its treatment from a doctor lodging in her house; in 1851 she went to Cruces, on the Isthmus of Panama, where she treated cholera with mustard emetics, warm fomentations, mustard plasters and calomel, and was called the "yellow doctress." [D]

In Cruces she had cholera herself: "I felt an unpleasant chill come over me … and, before nightfall, I knew full well that my turn had come at last, and that the cholera had attacked me." She recovered. [D]

In 1853 she cared for victims of a yellow fever epidemic in Kingston; she was invited by the medical authorities to supervise nursing at Up-Park Camp, the British Army's headquarters, and turned her mother's former lodging house into a hospital. [D]

At the outbreak of the Crimean War she went to London and asked the War Office to send her as an army nurse; she was refused. She paid her own way to the Crimea and, with Thomas Day, a relative of her husband, built the British Hotel at Spring Hill near Balaclava, a place of respite for sick and recovering soldiers; she nursed the wounded on the battlefield, sometimes under fire, and soldiers called her "Mother Seacole." [D]

She returned from the Crimea in 1856 in poor health and poor finances; in her memoir she wrote: "I returned from it shaken in health … a little labour fatigues me now--I cannot watch by sick-beds as I could--a week's want of rest quite knocks me up now." She described herself as "a hearty, strong woman--plain-spoken people might say stout." [D]

With unpaid bills and unsold stock at the end of the war, she was declared bankrupt in November 1856. The Times and Punch campaigned for her, a Seacole Fund Grand Military Festival was held in Kennington in July 1857, and her autobiography, Wonderful Adventures of Mrs. Seacole in Many Lands, was published the same month. [D]

W. H. Russell, war correspondent of The Times, wrote of her in 1857: "I trust that England will not forget one who nursed her sick, who sought out her wounded to aid and succour them, and who performed the last offices for some of her illustrious dead." [D]

She travelled between England and Jamaica in the 1860s and was back in London by about 1869 to 1870, where she mixed with royalty and acted as a personal masseuse to the Princess of Wales; she was painted by Albert Charles Challen around 1869 and sculpted by Count Gleichen in 1871. [D]
Her last known photograph was taken around 1873; little else is documented about her health or daily life in her last decade in London. [D]

Her memoir describes her lifelong practice of nursing and healing, including the remedies she carried, and her belief that the Creoles seek out "the simple remedies which are available for the terrible diseases": "beside the nettle ever grows the cure for its sting." [D]

list.item: Nurse, healer and writer; asked to be called Mrs. Seacole; known to many former soldiers and their families; still gives nursing advice to neighbours who call on her [S]

Widowed for many years, with no children; lives alone in rented rooms up two flights of stairs in Paddington; friends visit, but she goes out less since her fall and some weeks speaks to few people [S]
Income: a modest fixed income from savings and the fund raised for her; careful with money since her bankruptcy, and worried about the cost of medicines, a blood pressure cuff and taxis [S]

Her own remedies: ginger tea most days; a liquorice root infusion for coughs on and off; a liniment she makes with camphor and oil of wintergreen, which she massages into her knees; she shared these openly and wants them respected [S]
Diet: home cooking with rice, peas, fish, vegetables and fruit, and salted fish and pickled foods several times a week; tea with sugar; never smoked; a small glass of wine on occasions [S]
Strengths, supports and purpose: decades of nursing and healing, courage, humour, her writing and her friendships with old soldiers; she wants to keep walking to see her friends [S]

list.item: Headaches on waking for three weeks and blood pressure 184/102 mmHg at the visit (average of two seated readings with a large cuff); no chest pain, breathlessness, visual loss, confusion or weakness; fundi with arteriolar narrowing but no hemorrhages or papilledema; no hypertensive emergency; hypertension not yet confirmed: active, provisional [S]

Bilateral primary knee osteoarthritis, worse on the left: pain on stairs and on rising from a chair, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus and bony enlargement without warmth; clinical diagnosis without imaging: active, confirmed [S]
Fall risk: one fall in the past year, a trip on the outside steps without injury; afraid of falling and going out less; STEADI screen positive; Timed Up and Go 15 seconds: active, confirmed [S]
Obesity, class 1 (BMI 31.6); she calls herself stout and wants to lose some weight for her knees: active, confirmed [S]

Dignified, culturally safe care: address her as Mrs. Seacole; respect her expertise as a nurse and healer; ask about her remedies openly and check them for interactions without dismissing them; explain each choice plainly and let her decide; solve access barriers (a free home blood pressure cuff in a large size, transport, the stairs) rather than treat them as non-adherence. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); Licorice Root (2026) [S]

Confirm the blood pressure: home readings twice daily for seven days with a validated upper-arm monitor and a large cuff, technique taught; ECG, metabolic panel, lipids, hemoglobin A1c, TSH, urine albumin and blood count today; an echocardiogram for stage 2 readings with ECG voltage for left ventricular hypertrophy; treatment decided at the one-week review. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension, osteoarthritis and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]

Knee osteoarthritis: exercise therapy with a physical therapist, then a tai chi class at the community center; diclofenac 1% gel; a 5% weight loss; a cane, fitted and used in the right hand; no oral anti-inflammatory medicines because of her blood pressure and kidneys; a corticosteroid injection as an option for a flare. Guideline: 2019 American College of Rheumatology/Arthritis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hand, Hip, and Knee (2019); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension, osteoarthritis and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]

Falls (STEADI): screen, then Timed Up and Go, 30-second chair stand, 4-stage balance test and orthostatic blood pressure at visits; medicine review against the Beers criteria; vision and footwear checks; a home safety visit by an occupational therapist, with a rail for the stairs to her rooms; exercise for strength and balance. Guideline: STEADI: Stopping Elderly Accidents, Deaths, and Injuries (2026); Falls Prevention in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Interventions (2024); American Geriatrics Society 2023 Updated AGS Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults (2023) [S]

Her own remedies, checked with her: liquorice root can raise blood pressure and lower potassium, so she will pause it while her blood pressure is treated (her decision); ginger tea in food amounts is fine; her camphor and wintergreen liniment contains a salicylate, so it is used on a different knee or at a different time from the diclofenac gel, never under a heat pad, and kept away from the eyes. Guideline: 2019 American College of Rheumatology/Arthritis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hand, Hip, and Knee (2019); Licorice Root (2026); Ginger (2026) [S]

Loneliness and costs: a social prescribing link worker; the tai chi group and a lunch club near her home; a check of the help she is entitled to with costs and transport; generic medicines and a 90-day supply. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025) [S]

Lifestyle: less salted fish and pickled food, more vegetables and fruit, regular walking, and alcohol kept to occasions. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension, osteoarthritis and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]
